newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Deutsche Telekom sets high IPO range.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Deutsche Telekom sets high IPO range.

text.p: Europe's largest ever stock issue, the partial privatisation of German phone giant Deutsche Telekom (DT), will be offered to investors at a price ranging from 25 to 30 marks a share, the company said on Monday.

Backed by overwhelming demand from German private investors hoping to cash in on the sale of the state-owned company, DT at the weekend convinced banks managing the listing to set the price range at the high end of analysts' estimates.

More than three million Germans have already signed up to buy "T-shares", a fact that promises to transform the company's initial public offering (IPO) into a watershed event for Germany's financial markets.

"We have succeeded with the marketing surrounding the T-share over the past weeks and months of stirring up real "stock fever" in Germany," Telekom chairman Ron Sommer told a news conference at the company's headquarters in Bonn.

That demand boosted trading in the so-called "grey market" for Telekom shares -- in which brokers deal ahead of the stock issue -- where the price peaked early in the day at 39 marks before settling back to 35 marks by the end of the day.
And the rating of the Telekom stock also pushed up the prices of some other European companies in the sector -- like Denmark's Tele Danmark -- which rose three percent.
"If the indicative prices are achieved, then most other European telecom shares are undervalued," said one dealer in Copenhagen.
More than twice as many Germans have signed up for Telekom's IPO as Britons who registered for British Telecom's hugely successful listing 12 years ago, Sommer said.
Telekom has given Germans plenty of reasons to abandon their traditional aversion towards the risks of buying stocks.
Anyone who buys a T-share next month will be entitled to a dividend of 60 pfennigs, the full year's worth.

The company has also promised to pay a dividend of around 1.20 marks for 1997 and anyone who holds shares for three years will get one new share for every 10 held. Those who pre-registered can buy shares at a discount of 50 pfennigs.
The demand from private investors means institutional investors may be cut short if the IPO is oversubscribed.
Seeking to reassure international investors, Sommer said Telekom wanted to create a balance between German and foreign and private and institutional investors.
"Should the experts be right and the issue is oversubscribed, we will make sure that shares are fairly allocated," he said.

Telekom will float 500 million shares as part of a capital rise and banks have the option of exercising a "greenshoe" offering of 75 million additional shares. The German government will remain Telekom's majority shareholder until the year 2000.

Up to 67 percent of the IPO will be placed in Germany. As much as 18 percent will be sold in the United States, Canada and Latin America. Twelve percent will go to British investors, while Europe and Asia will each be offered up to eight percent.
The final distribution could change, based on demand.

With the price range set, Telekom will begin taking bids from institutional investors at a series of "roadshows" during the bookbuilding and subscription period that starts on Tuesday and ends on November 14.
Those who bid highest in the published range are the most likely to get a larger share of the issue, while bids at the low end could get squeezed out altogether.
"An investor must accept that if the final price is higher than the bid that he will receive no allocation," said Telekom finance chief Joachim Kroeske.
The final price for Telekom shares will be set during the weekend of November 16 and 17. Shares begin official trade on November 18 in Europe and the United States and a day later in Tokyo.
